title: She Plays a Deaf Hitwoman. Her Brother Produced It. Tomorrow, She Opens Opposite Alia Bhatt.
excerpt: Huma Qureshi's Baby Do Die Do is the scrappiest underdog in Bollywood this week — a dark, 18+ revenge thriller about India's first desi hitwoman, opening against the Spy Universe behemoth.
body:
Tomorrow, while the entire industry holds its breath for Alpha, a smaller film will slip into theatres beside it. No spy universe. No ₹150-crore budget. No Alia Bhatt. Just Huma Qureshi, playing a deaf-mute contract killer with twin identities and a revenge arc that would make Tarantino raise an eyebrow.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=2rQCZKoaEhc

Baby Do Die Do is the kind of film that shouldn't work — and that's exactly why it's interesting.

The Premise Is Genuinely Wild

Here's the setup: twin sisters, one of them deaf and mute, sneak into a five-star Mumbai hotel for a taste of luxury they've never known. They accidentally witness a gruesome murder. Before they can escape, the killer eliminates one of the twins. What follows is the surviving sister — the deaf one — transforming into a one-woman revenge machine, hunting down the man who destroyed the only person who ever understood her.

> "There were days when saying nothing felt much harder" — Huma Qureshi on playing a deaf-mute character

> "The reviews are mixed — Pinkvilla gave it 2.5 out of 5, calling the first half "painfully stretched" and the screenplay "half-baked." The pacing stumbles."

The film calls her Baby KarMarKar — "India's first desi hitwoman." It's a label that's equal parts absurd and thrilling, and it tells you everything about the tone this film is reaching for: crime thriller meets dark comedy meets something nobody has attempted in Hindi cinema before.

Huma Qureshi Is the Entire Film

Let's be honest about what Baby Do Die Do is and isn't. The reviews are mixed — Pinkvilla gave it 2.5 out of 5, calling the first half "painfully stretched" and the screenplay "half-baked." The pacing stumbles. The editing needed a sharper hand. Some characters veer into caricature when they should have been cutting.

But every review says the same thing about Huma Qureshi: she's magnificent.

Without a single line of dialogue, she carries the entire film on her shoulders. Fear, grief, rage, determination — all through her eyes and her body. It's the kind of performance that makes you wonder why she isn't getting more leading roles, and then reminds you that she's been choosing them herself. Huma isn't just the star here. She's also a producer, alongside her brother Saqib Saleem, through their banner Saleem Siblings. This is a family bet on an unconventional story, and regardless of what happens at the box office, the bet was worth making.

Sikander Kher is the other standout, bringing an understated menace to his villain that relies on presence rather than theatrics. Chunky Panday turns up dependable and solid. Seema Pahwa, as always, delivers with effortless authenticity. And Rachit Singh, the newcomer Huma personally championed — "The spotlight has finally found him," she wrote — gets a role that should have been more layered but still makes an impression.

The David Next to Goliath

There's something almost poetically unfair about Baby Do Die Do's release strategy. It opens July 3 — the same day as Alpha, YRF's mega-budgeted Spy Universe film starring Alia Bhatt and Sharvari. Alpha has the advance bookings (17,000+ tickets sold), the franchise muscle, the national chains, the billboards. Baby Do Die Do has paid previews starting tonight and a prayer.

But here's the thing about counterprogramming: sometimes it works. Alpha is targeting the mass action audience. Baby Do Die Do is targeting the people who want something *weird* — an 18+ crime-comedy about a deaf hitwoman navigating Mumbai's underworld, directed by Nachiket Samant with a visual style that owes more to Korean revenge cinema than to anything in the YRF playbook. These aren't the same audiences. The film just needs to find *its* people — in the metros, in the late-night shows, among viewers who scroll past the obvious choice.

For the Diaspora: One to Watch on OTT

If Baby Do Die Do doesn't make it to screens near you — and let's be realistic, Indian films with 18+ certificates and no franchise backing rarely get wide overseas releases — it won't be long before it lands on a streamer. Films like this, with strong performances and internet-friendly premises, tend to find their real audience after the theatrical window closes.

When it does arrive on your screen, here's what to know: the first hour tests your patience, but the second half catches fire. The revenge arc kicks in, the stakes sharpen, and Huma's silent performance becomes genuinely gripping. It's imperfect cinema — too long at 2 hours and 5 minutes, too loose in its first act, too reliant on one performer to carry structural weaknesses.

But that one performer is Huma Qureshi. And she carries it.

In a week dominated by spies and franchise spectacle, Baby Do Die Do is the scrappy underdog that deserves your curiosity — if not your opening-day ticket, then your weekend stream. Some of the most interesting films are the ones that arrive without permission.
